newsitem.title: USA: Missouri high court upholds tax hike for schools.
newsitem.headline: Missouri high court upholds tax hike for schools.

text.p: Missouri Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of a $310 million tax increase and new funding system for schools.

The ruling, released Tuesday, was seen as a victory for Gov. Mel Carnahan, even though the high court did not fully uphold the constitutionality of a 1993 state law that increased income tax revenues and created the funding system.
"We think this is a big win for the state of Missouri and for the school children of Missouri," said Chris Sifford, Carnahan's spokesman.

According to Robert Bartman, the state's commissioner of education, the high court found that a contingency clause in the law calling for a referendum on the tax hike under certain conditions was unconstitutional.
However, Bartman pointed out the court's decision on the contingency issue would not affect the tax hike or the funding reforms, which will remain in place.
"The plaintiffs won (on the contigency issue) but it had no affect," Bartman said.
Todd Akin, a Republican state representative from the St. Louis area who filed the lawsuit, was not available to comment on the ruling.
Akin had claimed a 1993 state law that increased state revenues in order to funnel more money to public schools violated the state constitutuion.
His lawsuit claimed that violation occured because the law contained a contingency clause for a referendum on the revenue hike and also covered more than one subject.
Lawmakers had passed the law in the wake of a Cole County Circuit Court ruling that found Missouri's system of funding schools to be unconstitutional.
The law included changes in the state's corporate and individual income taxes to raise the $310 million for schools, as well as changes in the foundation funding formula for schools.
Lawmakers inserted language in the legislation calling for a referendum on the income tax changes should the circuit court ruling on the state's previous funding system be ultimately overturned.
